title: 𓂋𓄿 𓏌𓅱 𓉐𓂋𓏏𓂻 𓅓 𓉔𓂋𓅱𓇳
titleEn: Book of the Dead of Ani — Spell 1, first half
work: Book of the Dead of Ani
workEn: Book of the Dead of Ani
draftNote: Draft — the hieroglyphs are read from the printed type of Budge's 1895 edition of the papyrus, and the signs and readings are still being checked; expect changes.
source: Papyrus of Ani (British Museum EA 10470), Plate V. Hieroglyphs transcribed from the interlinear text of E. A. W. Budge, The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum (London, 1895), pp. 19–20; Budge's transliteration and word-by-word English were used to check the reading of the signs and the sense, never for wording. Only the papyrus's own text is given: the passages Budge supplies from other papyri in his appendixes and footnotes are left out. Transliteration in the Leiden convention, with the reed written i; translation made fresh from the Egyptian. Shown left to right; the papyrus is written in columns read from the top down. The line under each word ("say") is the conventional Egyptological classroom pronunciation — a neutral e between consonants; ꜣ and ꜥ as a; w as u or w; ṯ as tj; ḏ as dj; ḫ and ẖ as kh; š as sh — an artificial teaching pronunciation, since the vowels of Egyptian were never written. The grouping of signs within a word follows Budge's type, which regularises the scribe's hand.
about: Spell 1 stands at the head of the long run of spells that follows the hymns to Ra and to Osiris and the judgment scene on the papyrus. Its red title names the whole collection, 'the spells of going forth by day', and says the spell is to be recited on the day of burial. In it the dead man, the Osiris Ani, greets Osiris, the bull of the West, in the words of Thoth, who says he has fought for Osiris and made him true of voice against his enemies at the trial in Heliopolis. This part gives the title and the first half of the speech (Plate 5, lines 1–13).

sentences.l: beginning · of · the-spells · of · going-forth · by · day
sentences.i: The beginning of the spells of going forth by day,
sentences.n: The papyrus writes the whole chapter title in red, the first three lines of Plate 5 (Budge marks the red with a line over the hieroglyphs). This is the first chapter title of the papyrus. ḥꜣt-ꜥ 'beginning' is the forepart of a lion, ḥꜣt 'front', with the arm ꜥ: a compound noun used for the start of a book or a list; what the arm adds to ḥꜣt 'front' is not clear. Its t is part of the lion sign's value and is not written separately. ḥꜣt-ꜥ m, with the owl m, is 'the beginning of'. rꜣw 'spells' is the mouth rꜣ with two strokes (the second a thin dashed stroke in the print, taken as a stroke). It is the plural of rꜣ 'mouth, utterance, spell', the word that heads each chapter (rꜣ n … 'spell for …'). nw is the genitive 'of' (the pot nw and a stroke), in its plural form to agree with rꜣw. prt 'going forth' is the house pr with r as complement, t, and walking legs as classifier of movement: the infinitive of pri 'go out'. m hrw 'by day': m 'in', and hrw 'day', spelled out with the courtyard h, the mouth r and the quail chick w, then a stroke and the sun as classifier of time. rꜣw nw prt m hrw is the Egyptians' own name for the book now called the Book of the Dead, and it stands as the Egyptian title over every part of this edition. These are spells that let the dead leave the tomb and go out into the daylight.

sentences.l: raising-up · glorifications · going-forth · going-down · in · the-necropolis · glorious · in · the-West · beautiful
sentences.i: of raising up and glorification, of going forth and going down in the glorious necropolis, in the beautiful West.
sentences.n: Still the red title. The next four words are nouns of action, like prt: four more things the spells are for. They are joined to rꜣw nw without a second 'of'. sṯs 'raising up, extolling' (Budge: seθes, 'praisings') is the bolt s (z), the tethering rope ṯ and the bolt again, then a post with a hooked top on a footed base, a man with his hand to his mouth (the classifier of speech) and a stroke as classifiers. The post is coded U39, the support that writes wṯs 'lift up', as the nearest shape; the identification is not sure. sṯs is the causative of ṯs 'raise'. sꜣḫw 'glorifications' is the bolt s, the crested ibis ꜣḫ with the placenta ḫ as complement, the coil w, and the man with hand to mouth and a stroke; Budge's line number 2 is printed inside the word. It is a plural noun from sꜣḫ 'glorify', the causative of ꜣḫ: to make someone an ꜣḫ, an effective, shining spirit. The sꜣḫw were the recitations that did this for the dead. prt 'going forth' is spelled as before, here with t after the walking legs. hꜣyt 'going down' is the courtyard h, the vulture ꜣ, two reeds y, t and walking legs: the infinitive of hꜣi 'descend', with its weak last consonant written yy. ẖrt-nṯr 'the necropolis, the realm of the dead' (Budge: Neter-χert), literally 'what is under the god', is written as in the hymn to Osiris. A slanting loop (coded D21, approximate) is taken as the r that completes ẖr. Then comes the flag nṯr 'god', written first out of respect, and the sign ẖr standing on its block; the t is not written. ꜣḫt 'glorious' is the ibis ꜣḫ with ḫ, t, the papyrus roll and a stroke. It is taken as the adjective, feminine to agree with ẖrt-nṯr, though ꜣḫ is mostly met as a noun (as in the hymns). m imntt nfrt 'in the beautiful West': m is the sign Aa15. imntt is the emblem of the West with t written twice and a hill-like sign as classifier (coded N25). nfrt is the heart and windpipe nfr with f and r as complements, t and the roll; the small cross at the viper's head is its horns. The pairs 'going forth and going down' and the West describe the dead moving freely between the world below and the daylight.

sentences.l: what-is-said · on-the-day · of · burying · entering · after · going-forth
sentences.i: To be said on the day of burial: going in after going forth.
sentences.n: The last words of the red title say when the spell is used. ḏdt is the cobra ḏ, the hand d, t and plural strokes. It is taken as the feminine passive participle of ḏd 'say', used as a noun: 'what is (to be) said'. It could also be the passive ḏd·t(w) 'it is said', with the w not written; the sense is the same. hrw 'on the day' (courtyard, mouth, chick, the sun and a stroke) needs no preposition: a noun of time can stand as an adverb. n 'of' (water n) is the genitive. qrs 'burying' is the hill-slope q, the mouth r and the bolt s, with a mummy lying flat as classifier (coded A54; the shape is not sure in the print). ꜥq 'going in' is the bird ꜥq with q as complement and walking legs. m-ḫt 'after' is the owl m and the branch ḫt, with the placenta ḫ and t as complements and walking legs; it is the compound preposition m 'in' + ḫt 'rear'. prt 'going forth' closes the title. ꜥq m-ḫt prt is one more thing the spells give: the dead may go back into the tomb after going out of it. The rubric ties Spell 1 to the funeral: it was to be spoken as the dead man was buried.

sentences.l: said · by · the-Osiris · Ani · the-Osiris · scribe · Ani
sentences.i: Said by the Osiris Ani, the Osiris, the scribe Ani:
sentences.n: The speech begins, in black ink. ḏd 'say' is the cobra ḏ and the hand d; the hand stands upright under the cobra's neck in the print. in 'by' names the speaker: the reed i and water n. ḏd in N 'said by N' is the usual formula before a speech. Wsir 'Osiris' is written with a long low seat (coded Q2, approximate) and the eye, without the seated god: the short writing used all through the papyrus. Wsir N, 'the Osiris N', is the title of the dead. Ani is called by the god's name because he hopes to live again as Osiris did, and the title stands before his name all through the papyrus. ꜣny 'Ani' is the vulture ꜣ, water n, three small strokes (not read), two reeds y and, as classifier, a kneeling man with his hand to his mouth (coded A2). The earlier parts code the same figure in Ani's name A51 or A1; here it is coded A2 from its shape, the hand raised to the face. It is the classifier of a person. The name is written twice. The second time Ani has his title sš 'scribe', the scribe's palette with water-pot and pen-case, a word-sign (Budge reads it ān). Ani was a royal scribe of Thebes. The repetition may be the scribe's, or a fuller restatement of who speaks; it is translated as it stands.

sentences.i: Hail to you, bull of the West!
sentences.n: The papyrus writes this greeting in red, and the red runs on to the next word, in. ind ḥr·k 'hail to you' is written as in the hymns. ind is the reed i, the sign nḏ (Aa27) and the cobra ḏ as its complement. Under the cobra is a low flat slab with a small tie on top, coded as the papyrus roll (Y1), the classifier; the readers could not rule out a flattened hand d. ḥr·k is the face ḥr with its stroke and ·k 'your': literally 'greetings to your face'. kꜣ 'bull' is a single sign, the two raised arms of the ka on a standard (coded D29), followed by a bull as classifier. The arms write the sounds kꜣ, and the bull shows that the word is kꜣ 'bull', not kꜣ 'ka'. kꜣ imntt 'bull of the West' is a direct genitive. imntt is written as in the title. The bull of the West is Osiris, ruler of the dead; the bull stands for strength and the power to beget.

sentences.i: says Thoth, king of eternity, (who is) with me(?).
sentences.n: in is the reed i and a sign printed like the red crown (S3), which also writes n. It is the last red word; ḏḥwty follows in black. in is taken as the verb 'says', which stands after the words it quotes, with the speaker after it. The pattern is the one of the speech-heads in the weighing of the heart, where ḏd in is red and the name black. So the greeting is put in Thoth's mouth: Ani speaks the words of Thoth, and the 'I' of what follows is Thoth. Budge renders àn 'behold', which in does not mean; in with a noun after quoted words is the regular way of writing 'says N'. ḏḥwty 'Thoth' (Budge: Teḥuti) is the ibis on its standard with t and two strokes y as complements. nswt nḥḥ 'king of eternity': nswt is the sedge nsw with t, n as complement and the seated god as classifier. nḥḥ is the wick ḥ, the sun and the wick again, without the n, the spelling of the hymn to Osiris. The title is given to Osiris in that hymn, so it may be addressed to Osiris here ('O king of eternity') rather than describe Thoth. im·i is the reed i and the owl m, the form of m 'in, with' before a suffix, and ·i 'me', the kneeling man with one hand raised. It stands with no verb. Budge reads '[is] with me'; 'in me' is as possible, the god being in the speaker who takes on his words. How it joins the sentence is not clear, and the translation marks the doubt.

sentences.i: I am the great god in the boat.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes n before m (water n, then Aa15 with a stroke; Budge: enma, marked '(sic)'); read m 'in'. Thoth speaks. ink 'I' is the independent pronoun: the pot nw (here for in), the basket k and the kneeling man as classifier. ink + noun is a sentence without a verb, 'I am …'. nṯr ꜥꜣ 'the great god': the flag nṯr with the seated god, then the column ꜥꜣ with the arm ꜥ and the vulture ꜣ as complements and the papyrus roll. dpt 'boat' is the hand d, the stool p and t, with a low barge as classifier (coded P1, approximate; Budge: ṭepet). The boat is probably the sun's bark, in which the hymn to Ra places Thoth and Maat on either side of the sun.

sentences.n: The first two signs of the verb are not clear in Budge's type: a round-topped slab (coded O26) joined by a line to a peaked mound with a small dome inside (coded N29). They may be one sign that the readers could not identify; the same pair stands among the classifiers of ṯmsw 'harm' in the address of Spell 125. Budge reads the word āba and renders it 'I have fought'. His transliteration has b where ꜥḥꜣ has ḥ, but no sign in the pair can be identified as either; ꜥḥꜣ is usually written with two arms holding a shield and a weapon, and the round-topped slab may be a misdrawn shield. The sense of the passage and the vulture ꜣ that follows fit ꜥḥꜣ 'fight', and the word is read so, but the reading is not sure. Two reeds after the vulture are not read (Budge's i), and Budge's line number 6 stands among them. A low sign printed like the sledge (U15) follows; as in the address of Spell 125, it stands for the forearm with a stick, the classifier of force, and is not read. Then come the water n of the sḏm·n·f, the form for a completed action ('I have …'), and ·i 'I', the kneeling man with one hand raised. ḥr·k 'for you, on your behalf' is the face, a stroke and ·k. In the myth of Osiris, Thoth stands with Osiris and his son Horus against Seth.

sentences.l: I · one · of · these · of · these · gods · of-the-tribunal · who-vindicate · Osiris · against · enemies-his
sentences.i: I am one of those gods of the tribunal who make Osiris true of voice against his enemies
sentences.n: The papyrus writes the demonstrative twice, nn n nn nṯrw; read it once, nn n nṯrw, as in line 8. ink 'I am', as before. wꜥ 'one' is the harpoon wꜥ with a stroke and the arm ꜥ as complement. m 'of, among'. nn 'these, those', the demonstrative, is spelled water n, the adze nw (approximate) and the chick w: a shorter form of the spelling in the address of Spell 125, which adds the pot nw, as line 8 does here. It is joined to its noun by n 'of' (nn n X 'these X'). The demonstrative is then written a second time, with two rushes and two waters (the spelling in the weighing of the heart). nṯrw 'gods' is the flag with a seated god and a stroke. ḏꜣḏꜣt 'tribunal, council' is the fire-drill ḏꜣ (coded U28, approximate) written twice, with t. A small pot between the two stands where the vulture ꜣ, the complement of ḏꜣ, would be expected; but the pot does not write ꜣ and the word is complete without it, so it is not read, as in the weighing of the heart. A seated god, a bar with short drops at the ends (coded N1, approximate) and plural strokes are classifiers. nṯrw ḏꜣḏꜣt is a direct genitive, 'the gods of the tribunal'; it could also be read 'the gods, the tribunal' in apposition. smꜣꜥ-ḫrw 'who make true of voice' is the causative of mꜣꜥ-ḫrw. It is written with the bolt s, then the plinth mꜣꜥ (a small bar inside the curve of the sickle) with the sickle mꜣ and the arm ꜥ under it as complements, the oar ḫrw 'voice' with the chick w, and the man with hand to mouth. It is a participle, with the plural ending not written. mꜣꜥ-ḫrw 'true of voice' is the word for the dead whose words were found true at the judgment. smꜣꜥ-ḫrw N r ḫftyw·f is to win N's case against his enemies. Wsir here is the god himself. r 'against' is the mouth r. ḫftyw·f 'his enemies' is the placenta ḫ, the viper f, t and the vulture standing for the ending -y, with a kneeling man holding a stick to his head (coded A14, approximate) as the classifier of an enemy, a stroke, and ·f. The plural w is not written, and the single stroke would also allow 'his enemy'.

sentences.i: on that day of judging the words.
sentences.n: hrw pwy 'on that day': hrw (courtyard, mouth, chick, sun) as an adverb of time, and pwy 'that' (stool p, chick w, two reeds y) after its noun. n 'of'. wḏꜥ 'judging' is the stand-like sign wḏꜥ (Aa21) with the chick w and the cobra ḏ as complements before it, and the papyrus roll. Between them stands a hand d that has no place in the word and is not read (the same spelling as in the weighing of the heart; Budge reads ut'āṭ). ḏdt 'words, what was said' is the noun from ḏd 'say'. Its first sign is a tall narrow sign on a small foot (coded U28, approximate), which stands for ḏ as in the introduction to Spell 125. Then come the hand d, t and a stroke. wḏꜥ ḏdt, 'the judging of what was said', is the hearing of a case. The day is the trial of Osiris against Seth before the gods.

sentences.n: The papyrus writes n and w with the kneeling man, without the k (Budge: nuà); read ink 'I'. Every other sentence of the speech begins with ink, and here the pot nw that writes in in ink is spelled out as n and w, with the k left out. The same writing comes again in line 10, so it may be this scribe's habit rather than a single slip; the word meant is ink either way. The next word is not known. It begins with a plain cross standing on a basin with two humps (coded Z11 over N26, both approximate), then t, the chick w, and the kneeling man, a seated god and a stroke as classifiers of a person or a god, and ·k 'your'. Read by their usual values the cross is im and the two-humped sign ḏw 'mountain' (Budge's ṭu), with the chick repeating its w: imḏw. The loaf t is not read. Budge reads àmṭu-k 'thy advocate', and his footnote offers temṭu instead; no such word is known to this edition, and 'advocate' is his guess from the sense, so the translation leaves a gap. The speech, in which Thoth fights and pleads for Osiris, suggests a title of a helper or champion. Wsir 'Osiris' is the eye, the throne and the seated god: the god addressed.

sentences.l: I · one · of · these · of · gods · children · of-Nut
sentences.i: I am one of those gods, the children of Nut,
sentences.n: ink 'I am', with a seated god as classifier this time: the speaker is a god. wꜥ 'one' (harpoon and arm ꜥ) stands in square brackets in Budge's hieroglyphs: it is his restoration where the papyrus is damaged. m 'of, among'. nn n nṯrw 'these gods': nn is water n, the adze nw (approximate), the pot nw and the chick w, as in the address of Spell 125. Then come n 'of' and nṯrw, the flag nṯr written three times for the plural. msw 'children' is the three fox-skins ms with s as complement, w, a stroke, a seated child (coded A17, approximate) and a stroke. nwt 'Nut' is the pot nw, t, the sky and a cobra as classifier of a goddess. msw nwt 'the children of Nut' stands in apposition to nṯrw. Nut, the sky goddess, is the mother of Osiris and his brothers and sisters.

sentences.l: who-slay · the-enemies · of · Osiris · who-restrain · the-rebels · for-him
sentences.i: who slay the enemies of Osiris and hold back the rebels for him.
sentences.n: The papyrus writes smꜣꜥ, with the plinth mꜣꜥ and the arm ꜥ after the sickle, the spelling of smꜣꜥ-ḫrw just before; read smꜣ 'slay', as the knife classifier and the sense require. smꜣyw 'who slay' is the folded cloth s, the sickle mꜣ (with the surplus plinth and arm), two reeds y, the chick w, the knife and plural strokes: a participle in the plural, referring to the gods. ḫftyw 'enemies' (ḫ, f, t, the enemy classifier and a stroke) and nw 'of', the pot with a stroke, the plural form of the genitive. Wsir 'Osiris' (eye, throne, seated god). ḫnr 'restrain, shut in' (Budge: χenrà, 'shut up') is the placenta ḫ, water n and the mouth r, then a reed i that is not read. Budge's line number 10 is printed inside the word. Then come two classifiers: a tall pole with a forked top (coded O30, approximate) and the low sign printed like the sledge (U15), for the classifier of force, as in line 5. The identification of the pole is not sure. ḫnr is taken as a participle like smꜣyw, with the plural ending unwritten. sbiw 'rebels' is the folded cloth s, the foot b, the reed i and the chick w, with a bent stick (coded T14, approximate), a kneeling enemy and a stroke as classifiers. ḥr·f 'for him, on his behalf'. The enemies and rebels are Seth and his followers.

sentences.n: The same two words as in line 8: ink 'I', written n, w and the kneeling man without the k, and the unknown word imḏw·k, which Budge reads àmṭu-k 'thy advocate', with the cross over the basin, left as a gap. ḥr 'Horus' (Budge: Ḥeru) is the falcon with a seated god. The speaker now turns to Horus, the son of Osiris, who took up his father's cause against Seth.

sentences.i: I have fought for you; I have gone(?) for your name.
sentences.n: ꜥḥꜣ·n·i 'I have fought', with the same two unidentified signs as in line 5 and the same doubt. This time no reeds are written. ḥr·k 'for you'. sbi·n·i is the bolt s (here a bar on a small two-legged stand, approximate), the foot b, two strokes y for the final i and walking legs, then n of the sḏm·n·f and ·i: sbi 'go, pass, travel', 'I have gone'. Budge renders 'I have made the defeat [of the foe]', a sense the signs do not give, and the meaning of the clause is not clear. ḥr rn·k 'for your name, on account of your name': the face with its stroke, then rn·k 'your name', the mouth r, water n, the man with hand to mouth and ·k.

sentences.l: I · Thoth · who-vindicates · Osiris · against · enemies-his
sentences.i: I am Thoth, who makes Osiris true of voice against his enemies
sentences.n: ink ḏḥwty 'I am Thoth' names the speaker plainly. smꜣꜥ-ḫrw 'who makes true of voice', as in line 6: the bolt s, the plinth mꜣꜥ inside the sickle, the arm ꜥ, the oar ḫrw. Between the arm and the oar stands a second, larger bevelled bar (coded Aa11 again, uncertain), which is not read. Here the participle is singular. Wsir r ḫftyw·f 'Osiris against his enemies', written as before. Thoth, the scribe and reckoner of the gods, speaks for Osiris at his trial, as he records the weighing of the heart for the dead.

sentences.l: on-day · that · of · judging · words · in · the-Mansion-of-the-Noble · great · which-is-in · Heliopolis
sentences.i: on that day of judging the words in the great Mansion of the Noble which is in Heliopolis.
sentences.n: hrw pwy n wḏꜥ ḏdt 'on that day of judging the words', as in line 7. This time wḏꜥ has the arm ꜥ after the cobra as a complement and the man with hand to mouth as classifier, and ḏdt has the same man and a stroke. m 'in'. ḥwt-sr 'the Mansion of the Noble' (Budge: 'the dwelling of the Old Man') is printed as one sign: a standing man with a staff, the official sr (coded A21, approximate), inside the enclosure ḥwt. It is a sanctuary of the sun at Heliopolis, named in the hymn to Ra. wr 'great' is the swallow wr with r as complement. Without a feminine t it may go with sr, 'the Mansion of the Great Noble', rather than with ḥwt. imy 'which is in' (the crossed planks im with m as complement and two strokes y) is masculine too, where ḥwt would want imyt; but the scribe often leaves the feminine t unwritten, so the translation keeps the place name whole. iwnw 'Heliopolis' (Budge: Annu) is the pillar iwn, the pot nw and the town sign. Heliopolis, the city of the sun, is where the gods' tribunal sits in this spell. The next sentence, which begins 'I am Tetteti, the son of …', opens the second half of the spell.
